overview.body:
**Thēseus** (*theseus*) — Heroism, Athens, Labours · The Gatherer (from τίθημι) — belongs to the Greek tradition, where it is catalogued under the domain "Heroism, Athens, Labours". The name means "The Gatherer (from τίθημι)"[^1].

**Thēseus** belongs to the Greek tradition, where it is associated with heroism, athens, labours.[^2]

PuniCodex restores the name as **Thēseus** and serves its temple at [theseus.com](https://punicodex.com/theseus/). The original carries both stress and vowel length, and exactly one historically valid Unicode restoration exists, which places the name in Tier 1. The plain ASCII form *theseus* survives as a modern convenience imposed by the early domain-name system; the restoration, not the fallback, is the form the project defends as philologically complete[^3].

sources.citation: Liddell-Scott-Jones Greek-English Lexicon, 9th ed. with 1996 supplement, 1940.
Wörterbuch der griechischen Eigennamen, 3rd ed., 1863.
Etymological Dictionary of Greek, 2 vols., Brill, 2010.

the-name.body:
The name is attested in Greek as **Θησεύς**. Etymologically it means "The Gatherer (from τίθημι)"[^1].

The reconstructed proto-form is *dʰeh₁-* (proto-indo-european, "to put, to place"). Greek Θησεύς, popularly derived from τίθημι 'to set, to place'; the Athenian hero who slew the Minotaur and unified Attica.

The ASCII form *theseus* survives only because the early domain-name system could not carry diacritics; it is a technological compromise, not an ancient spelling. The Unicode restoration **Thēseus** recovers the vowel length of the original directly in the address bar. The original carries both stress and vowel length, and exactly one historically valid Unicode restoration exists, which places the name in Tier 1.

The letter-by-letter transformation runs:

- **t** → **T** — Tau
- **h** → **h** — Theta
- **e** → **ē** — Eta: long epsilon
- **s** → **s** — Sigma
- **e** → **e** — Short epsilon
- **u** → **u** — Upsilon
- **s** → **s** — Sigma

The canonical temple for this name is served at **theseus.com**[^2].

sources.citation: Liddell-Scott-Jones Greek-English Lexicon, 9th ed. with 1996 supplement, 1940.
Wörterbuch der griechischen Eigennamen, 3rd ed., 1863.

pronunciation.body:
The reconstructed pronunciation of the name is **/theseus/** — Greek Reconstruction.[^1]

Phoneme by phoneme:

- **T** — Initial character of the restored form Thēseus.
- **hēseus** — Remainder of the name, preserving the distinctive marks of the Greek tradition.

For the modern speaker, the closest approximation is: 'THESEUS' — pronounce the restored form with attention to the preserved diacritics and length.

Kindred and historical forms of the name:

- **Greek** — Thēseus, the restored Unicode form of the name

Thēseus is Tier 1 because the Greek form preserves distinctive features that ASCII loses: stress, length, or special characters.

sources.citation: Liddell-Scott-Jones Greek-English Lexicon, 9th ed. with 1996 supplement, 1940.

original-script.body: The name is written in Greek as **Θησεύς**. This original script is the form against which the ASCII fallback *theseus* and the PuniCodex restoration **Thēseus** are measured: the restoration preserves its vowel quantity of the written form, so that a reader typing the modern address still speaks the ancient name.[^1]

sources.citation: Liddell-Scott-Jones Greek-English Lexicon, 9th ed. with 1996 supplement, 1940.

mythology.body:
The stories of **Thēseus** circulate within the Greek corpus, where the figure embodies heroism, athens, labours.[^1]

### Primary Attestation (Sources)

Thēseus is attested in the canonical Greek sources as a figure associated with heroism, athens, labours.[^2]

### Name and Meaning (Etymology)

The name means "The Gatherer (from τίθημι)" and reflects the figure's role in the tradition. **Thēseus** is the Athenian hero who slew the Minotaur in the Cretan Labyrinth and unified Attica under Athens. With Ariadne's thread he navigated the maze, then abandoned her on Naxos—an act that later tradition both criticized and mythologized.[^1] His career bridges the age of monsters and the age of civic law. His later deeds—including the battle with the Centaurs, the Calydonian boar hunt, and the Amazonomachy—made him the paradigmatic civic hero of classical Athens.[^2]

sources.citation: Wörterbuch der griechischen Eigennamen, 3rd ed., 1863.
Etymological Dictionary of Greek, 2 vols., Brill, 2010.

syncretism.body:
Thēseus appears within the Greek tradition and has influenced later retellings, artistic depictions, and scholarly study. The Unicode restoration preserves the name's distinctive orthography for contemporary use.[^1]

Within the Greek tradition, closely related names in the corpus include [[acheron|Achérōn]], [[achilleus|Achilleús]], [[adamas|Adámas]], [[aer|Aḗr]], [[aither|Aithḗr]], and [[ananke|Anánkē]].

sources.citation: Liddell-Scott-Jones Greek-English Lexicon, 9th ed. with 1996 supplement, 1940.

cultural-legacy.body: Thēseus continues to appear in scholarship, art, and popular reception as a significant figure of the Greek tradition. Restoring the name in Unicode returns the original marks that ASCII removes.[^1] Theseus became the symbolic founder of Athenian democracy and a recurring figure in classical tragedy, Renaissance painting, and modern retellings of the Minotaur myth.[^1]

sources.citation: Liddell-Scott-Jones Greek-English Lexicon, 9th ed. with 1996 supplement, 1940.

meditation.body: Thēseus embodies heroism, athens, labours in the Greek imagination. The name's restoration is not merely cosmetic: it recovers the stress, length, and script that make the figure recognizable in the source tradition.[^1]

sources.citation: Liddell-Scott-Jones Greek-English Lexicon, 9th ed. with 1996 supplement, 1940.

homeric-hymns.body:
The **Odyssey** places **Thēseus** in the underworld alongside Pirithous, punished for the attempt to abduct Persephone.[^1] The **Homeric Hymn to Apollo** presupposes Attic hero-cult and may reflect the Theseid tradition, though Theseus himself is not hymned.[^2]

His labours and synoikismos made him the Attic equivalent of Herakles, a figure too human for an Olympian hymn yet too heroic for ordinary mortality.

sources.citation: Homer, Odyssey 11.631.
Plutarch, Theseus 1–8.

epithets.body:
Thēseus is **Συνοικιστής** (*Synoikistēs*, founder of the synoikismos), **Ἡρακλείδης** (*Hērakleidēs*, rival of Herakles), and **Ποσειδῶνος παῖς** (*Poseidōnos pais*, son of Poseidon).[^1] Athenian oratory calls him **ὁ τῆς πόλεως κτίστης** (*ho tēs poleōs ktistēs*, founder of the city).[^2]

Each title reflects a different civic identity: unifier, hero, and divine son.

sources.citation: Plutarch, Theseus 24–25.
Thucydides, History of the Peloponnesian War 2.15.

oracle-sites.body:
Thēseus consulted **Apollo at Delphi** before his journey to Crete; the oracle told him to take Aphrodite as his guide, which led him to choose Ariadne.[^1] His bones were later brought from Skyros to Athens on Delphic advice, cementing the link between hero and sanctuary.[^2]

Delphi thus guided both his departure and his posthumous return.

sources.citation: Plutarch, Theseus 18; 36.
Pausanias, Description of Greece 3.3.7.

iconography.body:
Thēseus is depicted as a **beardless young hero**, often with a **club**, a **sword**, or **Ariadne's thread**, and in scenes of the **Minotaur's defeat**.[^1] The Athenian ship with black sails, mistaken by Aegeus for a sign of death, is another recurring image.[^2]

His iconography deliberately rivals Herakles, asserting Attic pride.

sources.citation: Lexicon Iconographicum Mythologiae Classicae (LIMC), s.v. Theseus.
Plutarch, Theseus 22–23.
